title: Universal basic income, after the trials

turns.speaker: Aiko
turns.text: The Finnish results came out years ago and people still quote them as though they proved whichever thing they wanted.

turns.speaker: Aiko
turns.text: Employment effects were roughly neutral, very slightly positive. Wellbeing improved noticeably. Both sides declared victory.

turns.speaker: Ella
turns.text: The trials all share a problem, though, which is that a two-year payment to two thousand people is not a basic income.

turns.speaker: Bruno
turns.text: Because you'd behave differently if it were permanent and universal.

turns.speaker: Ella
turns.text: Completely differently. You don't leave a job for a payment that ends in eighteen months, and nobody's employer knows either.

turns.speaker: Ella
turns.text: The whole-economy effects are exactly what a pilot cannot measure.

turns.speaker: Aiko
turns.text: The cost is the part that ends most conversations. Paying everyone a liveable amount is a very large share of national income.

turns.speaker: Bruno
turns.text: Though you'd claw it back through tax from anyone who doesn't need it.

turns.speaker: Aiko
turns.text: Which makes it a negative income tax with extra steps, and that's the version most economists actually prefer.

turns.speaker: Ella
turns.text: The strongest argument for me isn't the money, it's the administration. Means testing is expensive, humiliating and misses people.

turns.speaker: Bruno
turns.text: And the errors fall on the people least able to appeal.

turns.speaker: Ella
turns.text: Which is the case for unconditionality, whatever you call the scheme.

points: Finnish trial results showed roughly neutral employment effects and clear wellbeing improvements, which both sides claimed as vindication.
Ella argues time-limited trials on small groups cannot test a permanent universal scheme, since behaviour and employer responses would differ.
Whole-economy effects cannot be captured by a pilot.
Cost is the central objection, though clawback through taxation makes the scheme close to a negative income tax, which many economists prefer.
Ella's strongest argument concerns administration: means testing is costly, humiliating and misses eligible people.
Errors fall hardest on those least able to appeal, which is the case for unconditionality.
